root.note: The word reached Spanish from Mexico, but how the Nahuatl form was built, and even its exact form, is disputed.

history: Everyone agrees that chocolate came to Spanish from Mexico. Nobody agrees on what the word was. Its ending looks like Nahuatl atl, ‘water’, as in many Spanish words in -ate, and the drink was indeed made with water. The first part is the problem. The RAE's dictionary gives xocoatl, ‘bitter water’, but critics point out that the Nahuatl for ‘bitter’ is a different word. Corominas proposed a drink of ceiba and cacao. Others suggest ‘brown water’. Each idea has its objections, so we mark the origin as disputed. Spanish then passed the word on to Europe, where milk was added to the drink, in France, in the late 1600s.
historyEinfach: Chocolate came to Spain from Mexico. People there spoke Nahuatl. In Nahuatl, atl means ‘water’, and the first chocolate was a drink made with water. It was not sweet. What the first part of the word means, nobody knows for sure. Experts have different ideas. Spanish gave the word to other languages in Europe.

elsewhere.text: English took the word from Spanish. Cocoa is a different matter: it is a garbled form of cacao, also from Mexico.
